title: OIDC mTLS Client Auth + Certificate-Bound Tokens
subtitle: The client authenticates with an X.509 certificate and the token is bound to that cert — a stolen bearer token is useless without the matching key.

steps.label: Client holds an X.509 cert + private key
steps.lede: A confidential client is registered at the AS with an expected certificate subject/SAN (tls_client_auth) or JWKS thumbprint (self_signed_tls_client_auth). The private key never leaves the client.
steps.devtools: TLS client certificates live in the handshake, so ordinary browser DevTools cannot show them. To observe this flow you need a capturing proxy or a CLI trace like curl -v --cert client.crt --key client.key.

steps.label: POST /token over mTLS
steps.lede: The client opens a mutually-authenticated TLS connection to the mTLS endpoint alias and posts the grant. There is no client_secret and no Authorization header — the certificate is the credential.
steps.devtools: Note this hits the mTLS alias host (mtls_endpoint_aliases), not the main issuer. In the request body there is no client_secret and no Authorization header. In the TLS details of a proxy view, confirm a Certificate message was sent by the client during the handshake.

steps.label: Validate cert, compute x5t#S256
steps.lede: The IdP validates the certificate chain (or matches SHA-256 against a registered JWKS key for the self-signed variant), matches the registered DN/SAN, then computes the cert thumbprint that will bind the token.
steps.code:
x5t#S256 = base64url( SHA-256( DER( client leaf cert ) ) )
         = "bwcK0esc3ACC3DB2Y5_lESsXE8u9ie-mkDs5CdrEIYY"
steps.devtools: You can reproduce this thumbprint over your own cert: openssl x509 -in client.crt -outform DER | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '='. It must equal the token's cnf.x5t#S256.

steps.label: 200 — certificate-bound access token
steps.lede: The AS returns an access token whose cnf claim carries the certificate thumbprint. This is what turns a bearer token into a sender-constrained token.

jwt.title: Decoded access_token (RFC 9068 at+jwt)
payload: Resource server that must bind-check the token
Confidential client that presented the cert
Confirmation claim — binds the token to the client cert

steps.devtools: Split the access_token on . and base64url-decode the payload. The binding lives in cnf: "cnf": { "x5t#S256": "…" }. That value is base64url(SHA-256(DER(leaf cert))) — it must equal the thumbprint of the cert you presented.

steps.label: GET /accounts with the SAME cert
steps.lede: The client calls the resource server over a fresh mTLS connection presenting the same client certificate, with the bound token as a Bearer credential.
steps.devtools: The resource server recomputes the thumbprint over the cert on this TLS connection and requires it to equal cnf.x5t#S256. If a TLS-terminating proxy fronts the API, look for the forwarded verified-cert header (e.g. X-Client-Cert) the proxy injects — that is what the API bind-checks against.

steps.label: Replay without the bound cert → 401
steps.lede: The same token is replayed over a TLS connection with no client cert (or a different one). The thumbprint no longer matches, so the API rejects it. This is the whole point: a stolen token alone is useless.
steps.devtools: This is the key observation: the same token that returned 200 on the bound connection now returns 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token". Bearer theft alone gains the attacker nothing without the matching private key.

steps.label: Introspect an opaque bound token (optional)
steps.lede: For opaque (non-JWT) bound tokens, the resource server calls introspection. The response returns the same cnf.x5t#S256 so the API can compare it to the cert on the current connection.
steps.devtools: The introspection 200 body carries cnf.x5t#S256, exactly as the JWT did. The resource server compares it to the thumbprint of the cert on the current connection — same bind-check, different token format.
